text:
Before  reading  my commentary,  
1)Take in account  that I is only an opinion  . 

No matter the claims .. if there are no games specifically dedicated to that gpu, 
The gpu is gonna be a waste.. and don't  include the raytracing part .

Of course it will run the next wave of games,  but no games will target that 3080.  
Unlike console  . 
The disadvantage of a console  ,is the fact that a console can't evolve like a pc can do on a yearly basis.  
However, it might be one of it s strength.  
Since  there is only one gpu on a console for a long time ,  the developers can focus more on understanding that gpu and make the best to make sure all of the power Available is used smartly. 

On pc , there is some much variation of pc configuration ,to the point,  the developers needs to take in account  lower end average pc  configuration  while designing their gameplay,  the main benefits of higher end graphics cards bieng the boost in framerate and the raytracing capacity.  

The cheer diversity in the world of pc plays against the revolution of games . 
Or else ,if developers were to target  a  rtx 3090 specification it would  create  exclusivity ,not only,  into the pc ecosystem  but also among nvidia s other gpu. 
That would be really  bad for developers  who needs to have a maximum of people playing their games.


In conclusion:
The biggest advantages of the pc compared to a console ( evolving,  diversity) is their biggest disadvantage.  
For now ,the only way you are truly  gonna make your graphics card count, is into the world of work ( blender, zbrush,  photoshop, editing software in general, games creation.. ) 
Funny how a rtx 3080 is a better  investment for creating a game than for playing one on pc .
Don't get me wrong, the result are really  cool 🤯, in game , but it could be so much better if developers would fully use that  card specification . 

Hint at why a rtx 3080 would be a better fit for a console ( which is meant to be a game device that has to last a longer  time than a pc , 7 years in average)

Let's be honest,  everybody upgrades their pc  at least once in 2~4 years😇

text: The 3080 is targeting 4k gamers. Games like Cyberpunk, Control, The Medium, Horizon Zero Dawn, even Lego Builder's Journey can bring the 3080 to its knees. Especially on 4k/120hz tv's. As for next-gen consoles, they have less than half the power of the 3080. It results in games running at 30fps, or medium graphic settings, lower resolutions, no raytracing effects, etc. They just don't look as good as on a 3080. As for designing games for a 3080 card, that's where the settings menu comes in. PC games can run on their minimum spec and maximum spec, and use every bit of hardware in your machine.

“Massive leap.”

No. It isn’t.

The problem is that the previous gen, RTX 20xx series, had very little performance improvement over the GTX 10xx series. This was despite a large price increase. 

RTX 20xx delivered advanced features. But if you were focused on existing games, it was deeply disappointing, and atrociously expensive.

So when you’re talking about RTX 30xx series, you have to realize that the performance is only moderately better than the GTX 10xx series, which is 2 generations old, 2016 tech. But you get raytracing and DLSS.

text:
It does look like nVidia was correct to say you get about double the performance, as seen in benchmarks mainly utilizing the GPU.
Expecting double the performance with a twice as powerful GPU in any application that is also CPU reliant (and thereby possibly bottlenecked by the CPU) seems a little more than unfair.
CS:GO is an excellent example of this. No matter the amount of GPU power you throw at it, it's gonna be held back by the CPU because the game engine simply doesn't utilize the GPU to anywhere near its full potential.
To make an extreme example, imagine a game that does all the render operations with the CPU and the GPU only serves to display the game. No matter what GPU is used, the fps would be more or less the same. Would it then be fair to call nVidia out for not seeing double the fps?
As an end note, I partially agree nVidia's marketing could be seen as misleading, but we also have to apply some common sense here, and I wish Linus would have presented this a bit better.

text:
NVIDIA astroturfed this card so hard that farmers out here in Missouri had to till it under.
When I start seeing youtube videos hyping something and appearing ahead of my usual fanfare of political talk - there's big money feeding the algo.

Nvidia, however, has consistently been the embodiment of the rich kid who can buy equivalence.  The cuda architecture was a wreck that, ironically, was fixed by nvidia dropping cuda as a hardware structure and making it mostly an abstraction layer over the top of OpenCL.

Which is where Nvidia has always held the major advantage - armies of programmers who create oceans of optimized libraries.  Which is generally why they have been a higher cost card - they are constantly working to get things compiled with their tool sets.

And this shows with both intel and nvidia - whose primary markets have been animation studios.  If you take the time to find, say, blender's source code and compile it and your raytracing engines of choice for an amd cpu/gpu, let alone further optimizations in program design, you'll often see performance improvements nearing a doubling of performance - or greater, in some instances.

In short, this result was to be expected.  The curious thing is the low availability of the card.  This has not usually been a problem for Nvidia, as they have the capital to drive inventory.

This, coupled with their price drop would suggest that they launched prematurely, either refusing to announce a delay because of production shortfalls or, more likely the case, in an attempt to get ahead of an upcoming AMD release.

Graphics cards are super scalar designs and if zen2 and 3 are any indicators of AMD's capabilities in that regard, the implication for GPUs they release is devastating.

My guess is that Nvidia is more or less cutting their losses.  They have a solid improvement over their prior generation of cards, but considering the improved process should allow for nearly double the density and a 20% bump in overall clock speed, a mere technical doubling of performance indicates the card as an architecture is problematic at best and failed to achieve the project goals set out at the beginning.

AMD on the other hand has little difficulty improving performance via parallel architecture and has done so consistently over the past decade.  Even if AMD is building on 8nm like NVIDIA (despite the 7nm advertisement), chances are that the improvement in performance AMD sees will be more consistent with a doubling of performance or better, and Nvidia is pricing where they think they will be competitive.

Time will tell if they are appraising themselves properly.

text:
2:55 don't get the excitement there. It's 10 FPS difference. For me as an 2080ti owner it's just no reason to upgrade.
Why would I pay 700 dollars for 10 FPS? And when the 3070 claims to be faster than the 2080ti where does it come in?
Is it 5 FPS more than the 2080ti? 

Metro Exodus is another example of a bad performance compared to 2080ti. 
In 4k with DXR OFF + DLSS on it's 6 FPS difference. With DXR ON it's 9 FPS. Wasn't that the part where the 3080 should completely outperform the 2080ti?!
So when Nvidia claims that the 3070 is faster than the 2080ti, how much will the FPS difference be?! Like 3 FPS?
So the 2080ti is 26 FPS, the 3070 30 FPS and the 3080 is 35 FPS? Such BS. I think that the claim "3070 faster than 2080ti" is purely based on RTX + DLSS power. 

In raw FPS output 2080ti will put it to shame. Also the 3070 has like 8GB of VRAM. 
It also shows that even with RT on and DLSS on the 3080 has by far not enough power to play at 4k@60Hz/FPS in max. settings.
2x 2080 - what a joke. Nvidias marketing did well. Very well. They had me on their hype train and after seeing these gaming benchmarks I jumped off. Fast.
Thank god I didn't sell my 2080ti.

text:
@Linus Tech Tips Team:
I saw you mentioning your 3600 MHz RAM got issues with your 3950X - That's probably because of the BIOS version 2206. Try BIOS version 1302. :)
I got that board myself (with G.Skill 3600 MHz RAM) and I seriously (NO JOKE) swapped my RAM 3 times already. Each time when ASUS released a new BIOS that said "Improve DRAM stability" perfectly working RAM started to act up. The RAM itself works flawless with the previous BIOS version, but not with the new one. This is 100% reproduceable (I flashed back and forth a lot and was coresponding with ASUS support, but they stopped researching this). BIOS version 1302 is the best version in terms of DRAM stability & compability so far.
I currently run BIOS 2103 with a set of G.Skill TridentZ Neo F4-3600C14Q-32GTZNB @ 1usmus FAST Settings. 2206 would not run stable, not even on D.O.C.P (the RAM is on the QVL list).
Before that I was running F4-3600C15D-16GTZ @ 1usmus FAST Settings with BIOS version 2010 (2103 would not run stable, not even on D.O.C.P).
And before that I was running F4-3600C16D-16GTZ @ 1usmus FAST Settings with BIOS version 1302 (2010 would not run stable, not even on D.O.C.P).

text: @Netluxe TV Workstation and gaming cards are identical in hardware except a single solder point for the HID. The minor exception is for GXx02 level GPUs double precision floating point data paths aren't crippled (Titan and Quadro X6000). Workstation cards don't even have more memory anymore. The only difference is the driver and warranty. Radeon VII was sort of a Titan competitor, but it's real reason for existantce was simply the die shrink. AMD had a workstation equivalent, the Radeon Pro Vega II, but no one bought it because they couldn't remember the name. None of AMD's GPUs had crippled double precision float performance until RDNA.
author: @SeniorKlean

text:
@josemanuelperez2853  I don't think you read what I said correctly. I said "not really", not "real life". But yes, if you are doing a lot of double precision floating point calculations, a Titan would be better for prototyping your software than a 2080 Ti, but once it comes to actually deploying the software, Nvidia forces you to use Teslas for load balancing, virtualization, and automated maintenance.

I'd argue that you should just use AMD because they give 95% of the performance in compute for 60% of the cost (AMD frequently uses less power in compute workloads as well), but CUDA is much more developer friendly than OpenCL so total project cost may be less.

text: @bricaaron3978  That's a fairly substantial increase in a decreasing Moore's Law environment.  That being said, if you're someone like me that does video editing, rendering, art, AND gaming, I think it's a win/win.  And frankly, I doubt we will see as many increases this substantial for another couple years at least; my thought process is that Covid-19 will delay progress, and that this card is a mostly pre-Covid-19 accumulation of product/progress.  They've had this on the bench for some time.
author: @herakets3259

text:
​ @herakets3259  Moore's Law and Dennard Scaling don't necessarily apply to (embarassingly) parallel processing, though, which is what a GPU is. It affects maximum speed and power consumption, but there are other methods of increasing multiprocessing capabilities which I don't think are being properly explored for reasons I won't get into. I mean, look at something as simple as multi-GPU, lol. It's not like it's rocket science, and yet even that method of increasing performance hasn't been cared about and coordinated in the industry, and is now dead.

text:
Ray traced Minecraft IS pretty sweet...  Except, technically speaking, it doesn't exist yet.  Currently it is merely a beta, and it is of an inferior version of the game, the bedrock edition.  Furthermore, they are not giving it full support or attention, as it is MONTHS behind in updates.  For example, on September 3 the ray traced minecraft got its nether update, a full 3 months after the live versions got it.  And since then there have been 3 updates, which the ray traced version still has yet to get.  And they still haven't said anything, not a single word, about when or even *IF*, it will be coming to the more popular Java edition.

In short, do not be fooled into buying this graphics card just for Minecraft, you are going to be sorely disappointed.

That said, performance in Minecraft using shader packs and other various datapacks is going to improve with this new graphics card.  So it is not a complete waste.  Just, not what you may be expecting.

Personally, I will be upgrading to 3080 just before the release of Cyberpunk 2077.  Now THAT will be a game that utilizes the power of these new graphics cards, and well worth the cost.

author: @isanvicente1974

text:
@isanvicente1974  Its not a bandwith issue. Games generally do not need much in the way of VRAM, but when running they will pull as much as they can. You can see this if you pull a 6gb card and then a 12gb card. If you throw in say black ops 2, it will request nearly 6gb of VRAM on the 6 card and then nearly 12gb of VRAM om the 12 card, but the game will almost never use that much.
What bottlenecks the cards is the processing of the graphics information itself, and NVDIA is using AI to take lower resolution images and fill it in to a higher resolution. Basically the AI process a 1080p image and fills in the blanks to reach 4k. To be clear those arnt the actual figures, i just threw them out to better illustrate what i mean.
Also, the Ampere architecture is designed to pull straight from an SSD, which once games start developing around this technology will allow smaller games, faster load times, and less information moving back and forth.
Overall, the 10gb of VRAM has a speed of 19gbps, and the card overall has a bandwidth of 760gbps.
Whats going to limit the performance of the cards is going to be its actual processing ability and speed. I'm not too sure AMD will be able to outperform NVDIA at price.

It’s kind of depressing... One would think in the year 2020, we could have all the frames and pixels we want now. I figured we weren’t still challenged by bottlenecks in hardware like the 1990’s and 2000’s... turns out I’m wrong.
.
We’re barely scratching the surface of “playable” 4K PC gaming. 4K/90 remains a pipe dream for now... sigh
.
That PS5 and Series X consoles are much more important than I expected...!

text:
Make sure you look at details and multiple reviews, etc before coming to conclusions.

If you watch this video again and actually pay attention, you'll see that Linus largely proves the opposite of what he said. Instead of being up to 2x the power of a 2080, it's actually up to 2.35x, and that's with beta drivers, with a slower CPU, running older games/benchmarks that aren't designed to keep up with the huge leap in performance.

There will always be game to game, and benchmark to benchmark, and even setting to setting, variance. This is why multiple games, multiple benchmarks, and multiple settings are tested.

text:
I do appreciate that Path Tracing was written on the screen instead of Ray Tracing.
Path Tracing is in the group of rendering technology known as Ray Tracing, but when you say you Ray Trace something you are referring to a specific implementation in that group that is not Path Tracing.

The thing is Ray Tracing looks better than Path Tracing. You can get really close to having Path Tracing look at good as Ray Tracing, but you have to effectively render the image at 1000 times the size. 1000 times is not a number I picked out of my butt, it is the number that is used for movies and some TV commercials. Rendering a Path Traced images at 1000 times the size is still a lot faster than rendering a Ray Traced image, and the quality is close enough that it is now considered a waste of time to Ray Trace most 3D images.

text:
It was up to 2.35x faster. There's a wide range of factors that have a wide range of affects. Including that he was using a cpu that is slower for gaming, in games that were largely getting slowed down by the CPU. This is also with beta drivers. Plus, many games and benchmarks just don't have the capability to use the new power properly. ( Go load up the original Unreal Tournament and see how many FPS you get. It won't be anywhere near the tens of thousands you would expect. )

Over the coming months this will normalize a lot more to the truer performance of the card. This always happens with every release: It's just normally much smaller since the performance leap is normally much smaller.

This is the largest generation to generation performance leap we have seen...and it is coming out BEFORE the new generation of consoles, so we don't have the updated graphical demands of newer games yet.

text: Microsoft is doing the same thing, if you're running editing software the series x will run it better. But if you are running games, the ps5 will run it better. That's because games and editing software run differently and utilize different hardware configurations. It's easier to make a hardware configuration that runs editing software look better than a hardware configuration that runs games. For example the AMD ryzen 9 CPU's look more powerful on paper than their ryzen 5 counterparts, but if you ran editing and gaming on both CPU's the ryzen 5 would run the games better because of its higher clock speed (games prefer a higher clock speed over a higher core count) and the ryzen 9 would run editing software better (because editing software prefers higher cores over higher clock speed). In this example the ryzen 5 is the ps5 and the ryzen 9 is the series x.

text: @Pers0nman1  They don't have to work that hard to port stuff to PC, usually, devs make game assets once in various levels of quality to have in the PC version, and stick with a combination of a few for consoles. With Series S, they will have to scale down the quality of assets just to run the game decently on that box. This could make them work harder, which does hold back the potential of games, or they'll put out subpar versions of games on it, which will piss off everyone who buys a Series S. Either way that box won't last 6 years like a Series X could. The price difference won't matter when the system will get worse versions of games, require you to buy them from one storefront digitally, and be discontinued before the generation is over. It is not a good value whatsoever. Not having used games alone makes the system a bad buy. Remember the One S all-digital edition? No one bought it, and it was quickly discontinued. While they'll surely shift more units of the Series S than the One S all-digital, things are not going to look pretty. Xbox will be in a particularly tough spot considering their high-end box is $500. If PS5 lowers their price to $450 and $400 for the disc and digital-only versions, it'll be a tough sell for those not already locked to an ecosystem. I'm not saying the PS5 digital is a good buy either btw, as not having access to used games will make the cost of buying games more expensive long-term versus buying the disc-drive model with the extra cost upfront. Don't support digital-only consoles, they will never be a good value for consumers.

text:
Let's look at linus first statement logically.
If H(x) = hype 
We can negate H(x) with ~
We get ~H(x) which stands for not(hype). In this case, hype being disappointing. Our equation then goes
~H(x) ^ |H(x)|. Which means not(hype) "and" absolute (hype). We can continue from this statement and say 
~H(x)^|H(x)| - -> ~H(x)^|H(x)| here we have if not hype and absolute hype then not hype and absolute hype. Which is considered a tautology and is an invalid statement and  a fault of style.

​ @Rudenbehr  I'd say this is partially true.  It should say "It's not ONLY GPU intensive".  The game is definitely hungry for GPU cycles and VRAM.  The AI behind calculating the rendering for the cities on the fly is very CPU intensive.  Also, streaming in the live map/satellite imagery, weather and flight data is also very hard on your internet connection.  Constantly storing and deleting all of that downloaded cache data is also hard on your storage which is why Microsoft recommends using an SSD for this game.

This game is a good benchmark for your all around PC performance, not just the GPU or CPU

text:
So it performs exactly like the leaks from about 3 months ago said it would? Every leak from back in June/July about performance said the 3080 was going to be about 30% faster than the 2080ti and looking at the benchmarks those leaks were right on the money. This is about where most people expected it to perform. 

Now we just have to wait until the AMD release since a lot of the leaks on it said it was showing about a 40% improvement in fps over the 2080ti. So possibly AMD will have something that will beat the 3080 by a little bit and hopefully will have a good price on it. 

LTT, do us all a favor. When you get the 3090 we don't need to see and hear about it in every video card review going forward. NOBODY is going to buy it and throw it in their gaming PC. Steam hardware survey results should make it clear as day that NOBODY is gaming on 2080ti or any other cards that cost over $1000. You guys that get free cards for testing and reviews are the only people who use those cards. I know a single person in the real world with a 2080ti and he wishes he would have saved some money and just gone with the 2080 super card. Dr. Disrespect, Shroud, and other streamers who make tens of thousands of dollars a month will use the 3090. Those are the 2 groups of PC gamers who will have the 3090 in their gaming rig. Everyone else will be at the 3060/3070 level. That is where 90%+ of video cards are bought and that's where the focus should be, mid and lower tier gaming because those are the parts that will move a lot of stock. The 3090 is going to sit on shelves and gather dust because very few people are dumb enough to throw out $1500 on a single pc component unless its going to make them money in their profession. The fact that there are a hell of a lot of people still gaming on Nvidia 500/600/700 series cards should be a dead giveaway that the market for cards over $1000 is so tiny that it's not worth spending a lot of time and effort to give them content. 

I dread this every time new cards come out. Reviewers get free top end cards and then every build they make and review they do is hyper focused on that top tier card. NOBODY USES THOSE STUPID $1000+ cards. Quit wasting your time and ours and review the cards that actual PC gamers are going to spend their money on. Congrats if you get 2 free 3090s and SLI them in your "new personal build" but honestly I couldn't care less. The numbers will be amazing but we don't need them in every single review, nobody will be gaming on them unless they make a living gaming or with content creation.

text:
Two things so I dont continue to "rant" as I have for years: For everything tech related over the last 40 plus years, orders of magnitude  have been used to gauge things like RAM, CPU and GPU power, resolution, etc. And number two...I told yall not to give up them hopes.
Video gaming alone, following the order of magnitude increases, went from the low bits, to 8 and 16 bit gaming in the classic era from the 1980s onwards. Then 32, then 64 and technically 128 bit when the Dreamcast and PS2 came out. That being said...why has it taken so long for graphics cards alone to even go over 10 GB of power? FFs its 2020 not 2016. The one time I hate the tech crawl for not being faster and producing graphics cards a touch more powerful...ffs. Technology has often been many years behind where it should have been historically, and the proof is constantly there for anyone to discover just by looking at tech over the last 100 years. Hell just over the last few decades as I said before. By now the graphics boards should have already gone passed 16 GB for average consumer use. But fuck it...things should catch up this decade, but in another few years by 2024 onward ( I aint never wrong with my predictions. This also applies to phones finally becoming "useful" in my mind, though still no near " smart"). *shrugs *

text:
The one thing Linus doesn't seem to realize is going to be a problem is that the vast majority of people will NOT be buying those fancier, overengineered cards directly from Nvidia. They're going to be buying mostly from third party vendors like EVGA, MSI, etc. These things run HOT and suck up a ton of power. We're looking at another Fermi folks (in terms of power and heat), and people who get suckered into most of the AIB cards are going to get shafted. 

This isn't me trying to shill for AMD. There are huge question marks as to if RDNA2 will deliver the goods or not. My point is that you're going to be seeing excellent reviews for the Founders Edition cards, only for people to panic buy the "cheaper" cards because they think those cards will be able to run as fast. They probably won't. I think there's going to be a ton of thermal throttling. 

Wait just a little bit longer before biting the bullet. AMD probably won't deliver on the high end, but you might get screwed if you buy Nvidia in the lower tiers.

Thermpere is here folks. Don't bet burnt.

@Umetnik  I understand where you're coming from but it's important to note that high end graphics cards and "affordable" are kind of a misnomer. By their very design a high end graphics card is a luxury purchase. Except for people who render video for a living or do streaming video process editing, it is NOT something you "need" (and those folks don't care about price and will probably buy a 3090 or two). 

I understand that everyone wants to game and realistically a 3060 or 3070 are options for them if $800 is too much for the cutting edge flagship card. But it's important to note that even a 3070 is a luxury purchase at its $500 price point- it's something you're purchasing for an expensive hobby, treat it no differently than a $500 breadmaking oven or a $500 component you'll install in a go-kart. Treating them as a necessity and discussing whether they're budgetable and affordable is an incorrect paradigm.
